awd_titl_txt: POSE: Phase I: Enabling an Open-Source Ecosystem for Marine Robotics
awd_abstract_narration:
This Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems (POSE) project improves the accessibility and functionality of tools and software in the field of marine robotics. Marine environments present unique challenges due to their vastness, extreme conditions, and limitations in the ability to use technologies such as global positioning systems (GPS) and wireless communication that often facilitate terrestrial and space exploration. This project seeks to establish an open-source ecosystem tailored to marine robotics to address these challenges. The ecosystem provides a robust platform used for scientific and industrial applications, fostering collaboration and innovation across numerous stakeholders. The solution will improve the reliability, accessibility, and security of robotic systems through well-defined practices and tools that enable interoperability and quality assurance. This effort will ultimately advance scientific understanding, empower community participation in marine technology development, and support critical societal needs, such as environmental monitoring and/or fisheries management. By enhancing the development and accessibility of open-source software for marine robotics, this project supports the United States' leadership in science and technology, addressing challenges that directly impact the health and prosperity of the nation.

This POSE project focuses on the creation of a robust and scalable marine robotics open-source ecosystem. The project integrates and standardizes several existing open-source software frameworks and is designed with extensibility in mind, allowing for the incorporation of additional projects while addressing critical gaps in quality assurance. Key objectives include designing tools for project discovery and testing, developing a peer-reviewed pipeline to ensure high-quality software contributions, and documenting best practices based on community-driven standards. By strengthening the developer community and providing a framework for testing, quality control, and interoperability, this initiative elevates the role of open-source solutions both in marine robotics and in other fields facing similar challenges, such as space robotics. This effort produces outcomes that benefit the scientific community, industry, and society at large.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Modern oceanographic research increasingly depends on autonomous underwater vehicles, remotely operated vehicles, autonomous surface vessels, and other robotic systems. These platforms allow scientists to study environments that are difficult or impossible to reach by traditional methods, including under sea ice, deep oceans, and hazardous coastal regions. Although these robots rely heavily on software, the software ecosystem supporting marine robotics has historically been fragmented across institutions and projects, making it difficult for researchers to discover, reuse, and contribute to existing tools.

The goal of this NSF Pathways to Open Source Ecosystems (POSE) Phase I project was to develop a community-informed plan for establishing Open Ocean Software, an open source ecosystem that supports software used throughout the marine robotics community.  The project established the organizational and technical foundation for this ecosystem, with the long-term goal of improving the quality, accessibility, and sustainability of research software while reducing duplication of effort across the ocean science and engineering community.

During the project, the team engaged extensively with the community through 114 interviews representing academia, government laboratories, industry, nonprofit research organizations, startups, and students. These conversations identified the most significant barriers to wider adoption of open source software in marine robotics. Across these groups, participants consistently emphasized the importance of trustworthy software, improved interoperability between existing software frameworks, better mechanisms for discovering existing projects, stronger community support, and guidance for organizations wishing to release or adopt open source software.

These findings directly informed the design of the proposed ecosystem. The project developed a governance framework for an independent nonprofit organization, a maturity model for evaluating member software projects, a security strategy based on established OpenSSF best practices, and a framework for supporting interoperability, documentation, education, and long-term sustainability. The project also developed an online project directory, community infrastructure, member project standards, and governance plans intended to improve the visibility and accessibility of marine robotics software while reducing duplication of effort across institutions.

The project demonstrated that, despite differences in software frameworks and vehicle platforms, the marine robotics community shares a common set of needs centered on software trust, interoperability, discoverability, and long-term sustainability.  These findings provide an evidence-based foundation for developing shared infrastructure that benefits the community.  As a result, Open Ocean Software is designed to support a broad ecosystem of interoperable open source projects rather than focusing on a single software package, allowing developers and users to collaborate across institutional and technical boundaries.

The broader impacts of this work extend beyond software development. By lowering barriers to participation, improving access to well-documented open source tools, and promoting community standards, the ecosystem has the potential to make advanced marine robotics more accessible to universities, government laboratories, small businesses, educators, and students. These improvements can reduce development costs, accelerate scientific discovery, improve reproducibility of research, and help train the next generation of engineers and ocean scientists.

The project also strengthened collaborations among several long-standing open source projects developed at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Northeastern University, GobySoft, and other organizations. The resulting roadmap provides a practical foundation for establishing a sustainable organization dedicated to supporting open source software for marine robotics and ocean science.

Results from this effort have been presented at the MOOS-DAWG’26 workshop and accepted for presentation at the upcoming IEEE AUV 2026 conference, along with an associated publication in the conference proceedings.  To continue engaging with and building the community, Open Ocean Software will host a full-day workshop on open source software for marine robotics following the IEEE AUV conference and is leading a panel at the OCEANS conference in September 2026.
